Politics · Wildlife · Fukushima

The ballot boxes have bells. The firecrackers are for bears.

Fukushima votes for governor today at 1,085 polling places. In part of the prefecture, election equipment now includes bear bells and firecrackers—and the voting day ends early.

By Yuji Shimizu · YUJI @ Japan
Published October 25, 2026 at 08:15 JST · 9 min read
Voting and safety note · 08:15 JST

Fukushima City polling places are open today from 7:00 a.m. to 6:00 p.m.; the city says the earlier close is a black-bear precaution. Times differ elsewhere. Voters should use the time printed for their designated polling place, avoid poorly lit routes, and check the prefecture’s live bear-sighting map. Results were not available at publication.

At a normal polling place, the unusual sound is the dry scratch of a pencil. In Koriyama today, some election workers have another sound available: the crack of a firecracker. Forty-seven of the city’s 144 polling places are receiving firecrackers and bear bells because they stand in districts where black bears have been reported.

The equipment is not theatre and it is not a metaphor for a noisy election. Fukushima’s voters are choosing a governor on October 25 while the prefecture remains under an autumn warning for Asiatic black bears. The practical question for administrators is startlingly literal: how do you keep a route to democracy open when wildlife can make the walk unsafe?

Fukushima Broadcasting reported on October 22 that the prefecture had recorded 883 bear sightings and eight human-injury incidents during 2026. In Koriyama, an election official said workers would carry bells while watching the area and, after consulting the polling-place manager, could use firecrackers if a bear were reported nearby.

1,085polling places across and outside Fukushima Prefecture
47 of 144Koriyama sites receiving bear deterrents
7candidates—the most reported for this race

The election has not merely added a wildlife warning. It has changed the clock: polling places across the prefecture close earlier than the statutory 8:00 p.m. maximum, and Fukushima City explicitly says its 6:00 p.m. finish is a bear-safety measure.

The safest vote may be the earlier vote

Fukushima City opened its polling places at 7:00 a.m. and will close them at 6:00 p.m. The city asks people to avoid the dimmer hours around dawn and dusk. Local reporting says the close is one hour earlier than in the previous House of Representatives election; the city’s own page tells voters directly that the change was made as a countermeasure against Asiatic black bears.

The distinction between official hours and safe travel matters. A polling place can be staffed and legally open while the path to it feels risky to an older voter, a parent with children, or anyone walking from a rural home. Early voting therefore became more than a convenience. FNN reported that more than 250,000 people had already voted early by October 23, while reminding residents that every polling place would close earlier on election day.

Closing early also creates a democratic trade-off. Less evening access can burden people working on Sunday, even as it reduces exposure after sunset. The mitigation is advance voting, but that assumes voters receive the message in time and can reach an early-voting location. Wildlife management has entered election administration not as an abstract policy debate, but as a question of hours, staffing and routes.

Why the warning is no longer confined to mountain villages

Fukushima’s problem is not simply that bears exist in a mountainous prefecture. The range of reported encounters has changed. Governor Masao Uchibori said in September that 723 sightings had been recorded by the end of July, with seven incidents injuring ten people—already above the pace of the previous record year.

His explanation contained the more important geographic shift. Bears in Fukushima had traditionally been understood to live west of the Abukuma River. In 2026, sightings rose sharply east of the river in central Fukushima and in Hamadori, the coastal region, where municipalities had less capture experience and fewer established routines. The prefecture responded with broader surveys and stronger monitoring.

The previous fiscal year explains the sense of urgency. Fukushima’s annual-plan report counted 1,996 sightings and 21 incidents injuring 24 people in fiscal 2025, versus 618 sightings and six injured people in fiscal 2024. Those categories come from prefectural records and should not be mixed casually with a television station’s year-to-date 2026 figure, but both describe a risk that has moved into daily planning.

Japan’s Environment Ministry warns that national bear statistics are provisional and that prefectures count sightings differently. That caveat is important: one reported bear may generate several calls, while a map that accepts public submissions may not equal the police-derived official spreadsheet. Numbers measure reports and administrative methods as well as animals.

A map built for changing territory

On September 30, Fukushima launched a redesigned bear-sighting map with a public submission function. The prefecture says it checks contributed reports before adding them, and warns that the map total can differ from its police-based dataset. The map is a safety tool, not a real-time guarantee that a road is clear.

The advice is deliberately ordinary: inspect recent sightings, travel in groups, carry bells or a radio, avoid leaving food waste or unharvested fruit outside, and take particular care in early morning and evening. Firecrackers at polling places fit this logic of making human presence audible; they do not turn an encounter into something predictable or safe.

That point matters because the most shareable detail—the explosive packet beside a ballot box—can distort the story. The firecracker is a backup deterrent. It is not proof that a bear has entered a polling station, and it does not replace official guidance or police response. At publication, no such encounter at a voting site had been confirmed.

Official Fukushima Election Administration Commission video. This is the actual 2026 election campaign video, created with local design students; it does not depict the bear precautions.

Seven candidates and one unusually physical campaign

The gubernatorial contest itself is unusually crowded. Local outlets report a record seven candidates, including incumbent Masao Uchibori and six challengers. The formal campaign began on October 8 and ran for 17 days. Three prefectural assembly by-elections—in Fukushima City, Koriyama and Iwaki—are being held on the same day.

Fukushima Prefecture lists 1,085 polling places for the gubernatorial election. Counting begins after polls close, with Fukushima City scheduled to begin at 8:00 p.m. at NCV Fukushima Arena. Until the prefecture publishes its official totals, candidate claims, turnout projections and social-media posts are not results.

The previous gubernatorial election in 2022 drew 42.58% turnout, the second-lowest in the prefecture’s history according to FNN’s summary. That makes today’s shortened hours more than an operational footnote. Administrators are balancing a documented safety problem against an existing participation problem.

The word that connects the bell and the ballot

Today’s Japanese word is keikai—警戒, pronounced けいかい. It means vigilance, caution or being on alert. 警 carries the sense of warning; 戒 means to guard against or be wary of something. News reports use it for weather, crime, military monitoring and wildlife: kuma no shutsugen ni keikai suru (クマの出現に警戒する), “to stay alert for the appearance of bears.”

It does not mean panic. In this election, keikai is visible as a redesigned map, an extra worker, a bell, a packet of firecrackers and a clock moved forward. Those small arrangements show how public institutions adapt when the boundary between town and habitat shifts.

The final test comes after today. Election officials will count ballots tonight, but wildlife agencies must continue counting sightings, injuries and changing territory. If bears are appearing in places without experienced response teams, the solution cannot remain a special box of equipment used once every few years.

For voters, the immediate instruction is simple: check the correct closing time, use the official sighting information, and choose a bright, safe route. The ballot boxes are ready. The bells beside them explain why democracy sometimes depends on details no civics textbook imagined.
